src/application/transition-order.ts: the business rule is delegated to this.orderService.validateTransition(order.state, targetState) in the domain layer
src/application/transition-order.ts: `order.state = targetState; order.updatedAt = new Date();` sets entity fields directly. This is borderline (anemic model) but contains no rule logic
src/application/transition-order.ts: mapToResponse() maps the entity to the OrderResponse DTO, which is an application-layer job
parsedVerdict.reasoning: TransitionOrderUseCase.execute does the usual work of an application use case. It loads the aggregate through the domain OrderRepository port and throws a domain OrderNotFoundError if the order is missing. It hands the transition business rule to OrderDomainService.validateTransition, saves through the port, and maps the result to an application DTO (OrderResponse). The file has no persistence code, no transport or HTTP handling and no framework code. The state-transition rule lives in the domain service, not in this file. One weak point: `order.state = targetState` and `order.updatedAt = new Date()` set entity fields directly instead of calling an entity method. That points to an anemic domain model, but it holds no business rule of its own, because the rule is checked in the domain service. Mapping to a response DTO is a normal application-layer job. No ADR prose was given that would forbid this.
